title: SMTP Service Extensions for Transmission of Large and Binary MIME Messages
summary: Defines two SMTP extensions: one lets large messages be sent in chunks, and the other allows binary MIME content without needing to encode it as text. This makes mail transfer of big or binary messages simpler. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Sending a big package is easier if you can send it in labeled boxes and do not have to translate it first. This lets email servers do that.

questions: how to send binary mime over smtp
subtitle: Two SMTP extensions: send mail in length-prefixed chunks with BDAT, and send raw binary MIME with no text encoding.

tldr.problem: SMTP's DATA command makes both sides scan a large message for the end-of-message marker, and binary content has to be inflated by base64 or quoted-printable encoding.
tldr.mechanism: CHUNKING adds a BDAT command that states each chunk's exact length in octets, so no scanning is needed. BINARYMIME builds on it to let a MIME message with the binary transfer encoding travel unencoded.
tldr.outcome: Servers that advertise CHUNKING and BINARYMIME in their EHLO reply can accept large and binary messages directly. This RFC obsoletes the experimental RFC 1830 and is on the standards track.

today: RFC 3030 is a Proposed Standard and is not marked as obsoleted or updated in the metadata. It obsoletes RFC 1830.

sections.title: Why Mail Needed Chunks and Binary
sections.content:
RFC 3030 defines two extensions to the SMTP service. The first, CHUNKING, lets a client and server use an alternative to the DATA command called BDAT. The second, BINARYMIME, uses BDAT to allow MIME messages that employ the binary transfer encoding.

The RFC gives two motivations. Large MIME messages are expected, and there is a performance-based desire to stop scanning every message for the CR LF . CR LF sequence that marks its end. Separately, Internet mail is increasingly multimedia, and the overhead of base64 and quoted-printable encoding should be avoided between hosts that can process binary messages.

Both extensions use the SMTP service extension mechanism: the receiver (receiver-SMTP) declares support, and the sender (sender-SMTP) is then free to use it. The work obsoletes RFC 1830, which had been experimental because of doubts about how robust the binary encoding was in deployed MIME software.
sections.eli5: Email used to need a special 'the end' marker that everyone had to hunt for, and pictures had to be translated into letters first. These two add-ons fix both problems.

sections.title: The CHUNKING Extension and BDAT
sections.content:
A server offers the extension by including the EHLO keyword CHUNKING in a 250 reply. The client then sends the message as a series of BDAT commands. Each takes the exact length of the chunk in octets, and an optional LAST marker on the final chunk. The grammar is BDAT SP chunk-size [ SP end-marker ] CR LF.

The message data follows immediately after the command line, and the receiver returns a 250 reply once it has the specified number of octets. The last BDAT MAY have a byte count of zero. Servers that offer BDAT MUST still support DATA, and the extension can be used for 7-bit, 8BITMIME or BINARYMIME messages. It may also be used for message submission.

Byte counting is critical. If the stated size is too large, the receiver keeps waiting or reads the next command as data. If it is too small, the rest of the data is parsed as invalid commands, so parsers MUST be prepared to reject lines of arbitrary octets. Text sent with BDAT MUST be in canonical MIME format with lines ending in CR LF, and chunking lets a sender convert and count one chunk at a time.

The receiver does not acknowledge the BDAT command itself before the data is sent. Sending BDAT to a server that did not advertise CHUNKING makes it parse the data as a possibly very long command line containing binary data.
sections.eli5: Instead of ending a long letter with a special sign-off, you write on each box how many pages are inside. The receiver counts pages and knows exactly when a box is done.

sections.title: Errors, Sequencing and Reset
sections.content:
A 250 response MUST be sent for each successful BDAT block. If a failure occurs after a BDAT is received, the receiver MUST accept and discard the associated data before sending the 4XX or 5XX code. When the sender sees such a code, the transaction is failed and it MUST NOT send further BDAT segments. If the receiver supports command pipelining, it MUST be ready to discard chunks already in the pipeline.

Any BDAT after BDAT LAST is illegal and MUST get a 503 'Bad sequence of commands' reply. The state after a failed BDAT or such an error is indeterminate, so the sender MUST send RSET to clear the transaction. RSET sent after the first BDAT and before BDAT LAST clears all segments sent in that transaction.

DATA and BDAT cannot be mixed in one transaction; a DATA after a BDAT also gets a 503. Using both in the same session is allowed as long as they are in different transactions.
sections.eli5: If a box turns out to be bad, the receiver still takes it off your hands, tells you there is a problem, and you stop sending. To start over you say 'reset' first.

sections.title: The BINARYMIME Extension
sections.content:
The EHLO keyword BINARYMIME takes no parameter and can only be used together with CHUNKING. It adds a new value to the BODY parameter of the MAIL command defined for 8-bit MIME, so the value becomes 7BIT, 8BITMIME or BINARYMIME. No new verbs are defined, and the maximum length of a MAIL FROM line grows by 16 characters.

When a receiver accepts BODY=BINARYMIME, it agrees to preserve all bits in each octet sent with BDAT, and it MUST deliver or relay the message so those bits are preserved. BINARYMIME cannot be used with DATA; a DATA after such a MAIL gets a 503 reply.

The sender must make sure the MIME message is well formed. Text MUST be in canonical encoding with each line ended by CR LF, and any local-storage transformation MUST be reversed before sending. The ban on UTF-16 within the text top-level media type still applies.
sections.eli5: The receiver promises to hand your package along exactly as it came, no changes. In return, you promise to pack it the standard way.

sections.title: When the Receiver Cannot Take Binary
sections.content:
If a receiver does not indicate BINARYMIME support, the sender MUST NOT, under any circumstances, send binary data. For a message that uses the binary encoding, the sender has three options: convert it to valid 8-bit MIME (if the receiver supports the 8-bit extension and the content suits it), convert it to valid 7-bit MIME, or treat it as a permanent delivery failure.

Any conversion MUST cause no loss of information and MUST produce valid 7-bit or 8-bit MIME, with no nested base64 or quoted-printable encodings. The RFC notes that at the time of writing there is no mechanism for converting binary MIME to 8-bit MIME, because that would need a new content-transfer-encoding.

If a message has the binary content-transfer-encoding but the BODY parameter does not say BINARYMIME, the message MUST be accepted, and SHOULD be returned to the sender with an appropriate DSN.
sections.eli5: If the other side cannot handle raw packages, you must translate it into a safe form or tell the sender it cannot be delivered. You may never just send it anyway.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC shows two dialogues. In the first, a client sends an 86-octet message to one recipient with a single BDAT 86 LAST after the server advertised CHUNKING. The server answers 250 after receiving the octets.

In the second, the server advertises PIPELINING, BINARYMIME and CHUNKING. The client pipelines MAIL FROM with BODY=BINARYMIME and two RCPT commands, then sends BDAT 100000, BDAT 324 and BDAT 0 LAST. The server replies 250 to each chunk and a final 250 saying 100324 octets were received.
sections.eli5: One example sends a tiny note in one box. The other sends a huge parcel in two boxes plus an empty 'that is all' box.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the extensions are not known to present any additional security issues beyond those already endemic to electronic mail, present in conforming SMTP implementations, or otherwise made possible by MIME.

It does not add any security mechanism of its own.
sections.eli5: These add-ons do not make email any safer or less safe than it already was.
